title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how students’ voluntary use of elaborated feedback in an online physics learning platform relates to later learning outcomes. The authors are motivated by the design problem of adaptive feedback systems: when learners are given both simple verification feedback and richer, multimodal explanations, which feedback formats do they choose, and do those choices associate with better performance? The study is also positioned as relevant to emerging AI-enabled tutoring systems and multimodal large language models, because it informs how feedback could be tailored across verbal, graphical, and mathematical representations.

The intervention/approach was a computer-based platform (KI4SCool) that delivered immediate verification feedback after multiple-choice kinematics questions and optional elaborated feedback in three external representations: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. Students could open any combination of these representations, and the researchers logged their feedback-selection behavior. The study used a prospective observational cohort design rather than random assignment. Participants were high school students in grades 10–11 at schools across Germany, split into two cohorts with slightly different pre/post-test designs, and data were collected over approximately one term (16–24 weeks). In total, 661 students who completed both pre- and post-tests and answered at least one exercise were analyzed.

The main findings were that greater use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test scores, even after controlling for prior knowledge, platform performance, exercise count, and confidence. However, the authors stress that this is correlational and cannot establish causality. Clustering analyses suggested four broad feedback-use groups, including students who never opened elaborated feedback, those who frequently used all three formats, those who favored verbal feedback, and those who used a more balanced mix. Time-resolved sequences did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy differences beyond frequency of feedback use. Overall, the study suggests that multimodal elaborated feedback can support learning in high school physics, but the benefits may depend more on how often students engage with feedback than on a distinct time-based strategy pattern.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational cohort study with mixed-effects and ANCOVA analyses, but it is not randomized and cannot support causal claims about the feedback intervention. The design has moderate credibility for associational evidence, with some concern about confounding and attrition.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed association between elaborated feedback use and post-test performance is small but positive (standardized β≈0.08-0.13), which fits a modest impact profile. The findings are relevant for a K-12 science population, though they are correlational rather than causal.

interventions.use_case: Computer-based physics practice platform (KI4SCool) delivering verification feedback after multiple-choice kinematics items, with optional elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical formats.
Prototype evidence for adaptive tutoring design using learner profiles and multiple external representations to tailor feedback elaboration and representational format in physics.

finding.finding_summary: In an observational study of high school physics students (n=661), greater use of elaborated multimodal feedback was associated with higher post-test performance. In the mixed-effects models, feedback frequency had a small positive standardized association with post-test scores in Cohort 1 (β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]) and Cohort 2 (β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054), controlling for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence.

The paper found that students used distinct feedback-selection strategies and that some patterns related weakly to learning, but the sequence-based analysis did not reveal meaningful time-resolved strategy differences. In Cohort 2, only one cluster showed a significant positive slope between feedback frequency and post-test performance (estimate=33.83, SE=13.02, p=.010), while other cluster comparisons were non-significant or only trends.
finding.measure: Feedback-selection strategy clusters; association with post-test performance
finding.study_size: n=661 overall; n=192 for time-resolved sequence analysis
finding.effect_size: estimate=33.83 in one cluster; cluster contrast trend p=.0597
